jokes.label: Joke A
jokes.title: Trust Exercise
jokes.joke: I tried acting once, and the director said, “In this scene, just fall backward and trust your co-star will catch you.” That’s when I learned acting isn’t lying convincingly; it’s finding out which stranger has been nodding through rehearsal like he read the email. He missed me completely. Great performance, though — I really believed he cared.

jokes.label: Joke B
jokes.title: Method Acting the GPS
jokes.joke: I was in an acting class and the teacher said, 'Commit fully to the role — no matter what, stay in character.' So I played an optimist for a week. Someone told me my car got towed. I said, 'That's amazing — free valet!' My girlfriend left me. 'She's giving me time to grow!' I got fired. I still haven't broken character. I genuinely think this is going great.

jokes.label: Joke C
jokes.title: The Blurry Extra
jokes.joke: I envy the optimism of struggling actors. My buddy has been a blurry background extra in exactly one regional mayonnaise commercial, but he still lives like he's dodging paparazzi. I went to his apartment and all his blinds were drawn. I asked, 'Is the sun in your eyes?' He whispered, 'No, the fans found my address.' I looked out the window. It was just a raccoon trying to open a yogurt container.

jokes.label: Joke D
jokes.title: Blind Trust in the Studio
jokes.joke: I went to this photographer's studio last month. You stand there under the lights, having to blindly trust the guy behind the camera with your whole image. He's yelling, 'Chin up! Eyes this way!' I'm smiling like an idiot, thinking this is gonna be gold. Got the prints back yesterday – I look like I lost a fight with a wind tunnel. Turns out the only thing I nailed was trusting the wrong artist.

jokes.label: Joke E
jokes.title: Blind Trust Issues
jokes.joke: I once dated an actor who said I should "trust the process," which is terrifying when their whole job is pretending to be someone else. I’d ask how their day was, and they’d pause like they were waiting for a director to yell cut. Nothing makes you question your life choices like realizing you’re emotionally invested in a person who might still be in character.

premise.headline: A background actor prepares for the world’s least glamorous fan encounter.

featureImagePrompt:
Generate one polished web feature image for Paperclipalypse.

ASPECT RATIO: exactly 2:1, horizontal wide banner, 1024x506 preview preferred.

Style: full-color gothic newspaper-comic illustration, darkly funny but warm, clean black ink, crisp editorial cartoon linework, cinematic stage lighting, high contrast, readable composition. Not monochrome. Not sepia-only. Use warm amber stage lights, dark bronze and silver metal, muted apartment blues and greens, dusty blue-gray shadows, cream-white text, and subtle deep red accents.

Composition: divide the picture visually into three natural areas without writing labels. On the left side, show a charming anthropomorphic metallic paperclip stand-up comedian standing upright on a small wooden comedy stage at a vintage microphone. In the center, show a cramped but normal urban apartment interior with believable perspective. On the right side, show a dark framed poster panel containing the joke text.

Scene details: a struggling actor stands in a modest apartment with blinds partly drawn, looking overly serious and secretive as if avoiding fame. Through the window, show the harmless final reveal outside: a small raccoon fussing with a yogurt container near a trash can or stoop, while the actor dramatically mistakes it for intense public attention. Include ordinary props such as blinds, a couch, a small table, an unpaid headshot/photo, and city-window lighting.

Physical layout rules:
- Keep all people, furniture, windows, blinds, props, and the stage grounded with believable perspective.
- Do not place anyone inside a wall, window frame, couch, drawer, box, or impossible room.
- Do not create floating furniture, duplicate limbs, warped hands, objects passing through bodies, or impossible window geometry.
- Do not show actual paparazzi crowds, camera flashes, brand logos, horror, violence, or unsafe content.
- Keep the scene funny, non-gory, and focused on comic overreaction.

Visible text allowed in the entire image: the right-panel joke text, a tiny stage sign reading Paperclipalypse, and optionally a small winner/title header above the right panel. Do not render any other words. In particular, do not write LEFT, CENTER, RIGHT, ZONE, composition notes, prompt labels, layout labels, percentages, watermarks, signatures, fake captions, brand names, or filler microtext anywhere in the image.

Optional small header text above the panel: Winner: Gemini Flash - The Blurry Extra

Exact joke text to render in the right panel:
I envy the optimism of struggling actors. My buddy has been a blurry background extra in exactly one regional mayonnaise commercial, but he still lives like he's dodging paparazzi. I went to his apartment and all his blinds were drawn. I asked, 'Is the sun in your eyes?' He whispered, 'No, the fans found my address.' I looked out the window. It was just a raccoon trying to open a yogurt container.

Scene source: use the winning joke as the only scene brief. Do not infer a separate premise from all six seed terms.

Text rules: use simple clean lettering, spell every word correctly, keep the text inside the right panel, and do not distort letter shapes. The website HTML remains the canonical exact joke text if image lettering is imperfect.

The final image should feel like a finished feature image for an AI comedy tournament: funny, stylish, readable, full-color, visually balanced, physically possible, and free of prompt/layout labels.
